title: Angle Relationships

findings.finding: Students must select a reflex turn before reflex angles have been introduced.
findings.breakdown: The three-letter naming rule identifies the arms but does not explain how “reflex” changes the turn students must mark.
findings.checked: The preceding teaching in p3, p5 and p6 contains no reflex-angle explanation. The definition and major-arc illustration in p12-reflex come after these questions. Removed p9-q6-d from the targets: its supplied arc already identifies the bounding arms needed for naming.
findings.assumptions: Selecting a reflex turn is a new variant of the angle conventions being taught.

repair.proposal: Before p7-q2-j, add: “Two arms bound two turns. A reflex angle is the larger turn, greater than 180° and less than 360°. For these questions, unless reflex is specified, mark the smaller turn.” Illustrate the contrast using the same arms BF and BC in parts i and j.

findings.doneWhen: Students see how the reflex qualifier changes the selected turn while the arms and vertex remain unchanged.

findings.finding: The complete angle-naming task in p6-guided-d is repeated unchanged in p9-q6-a.
findings.breakdown: Both tasks use vertex D, arms DC, DE and DF, and the marked sector between DE and DF, producing the same angle names without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared both instructions and complete diagram specifications. Each asks students to name the marked angle; no instructional purpose for the unchanged copy is stated.
findings.assumptions: Students complete the guided practice before the later exercise.

repair.proposal: In p9-q6-a, retain the diagram and marked sector but relabel D as P, C as Q, E as R and F as S. The marked angle is then ∠RPS or ∠SPR.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains the same task structure with different labels and the answers ∠RPS or ∠SPR.

findings.finding: Add a numerical comparison across the right-angle and straight-angle boundaries.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes the difference between an exact boundary and values on either side.
findings.checked: All classifications follow p12-classification. The existing numerical practice contains boundary values but no consecutive comparison across them.
findings.assumptions: Students use the classifications already taught on p12.

repair.proposal: After p14-q2-l, add one instruction: “Predict how the classification changes as the angle increases.” Append m) 89° [acute], n) 90° [right], o) 91° [obtuse], p) 180° [straight], q) 181° [reflex], followed by unpatterned r) 247° [reflex]. Only the angle magnitude varies; the representation and classification task remain fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The five-part run and unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing classification instruction.

findings.finding: Compare the complement and supplement calculated for two existing rows.
findings.breakdown: Students connect their consistent difference with the difference between the two required totals.
findings.checked: For 25°, the partners are 65° and 155°; for 79°, they are 11° and 101°. Both differences are 90°. The explanation uses the definitions on p16.
findings.assumptions: Students have completed the existing table.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (a) For the 25° row, how much larger is the supplement than the complement? [90°] (b) For the 79° row, how much larger is the supplement than the complement? [90°] (c) Explain why these differences are equal. [In each row the same angle is subtracted from 180° and 90°, so the results differ by 90°.]

findings.doneWhen: The extension follows the existing table, with one question in each part.

findings.finding: Question 3 requires angle addition and subtraction before the general angle part-whole relationship has been taught.
findings.breakdown: Students must identify an outer arc as the whole and distinguish finding that whole from finding a missing component. Adjacency identification alone does not establish this numerical relationship.
findings.checked: p19 teaches common vertex, common arm and non-overlap. Earlier p16 teaching adds separate angles to classify stipulated totals; it does not model a combined angle or a missing component of an arbitrary total. p21-q3-a–d require combining sectors, while e–h require finding a component.
findings.assumptions: Whole-number addition and subtraction are prior knowledge; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p21-q3, add: “The sizes of adjacent angles add to the size of the whole angle they form. To find a missing part, subtract the known part from the whole.” Show sectors 32° and 47° with an outer arc t° and write t = 32 + 47 = 79°. Then show the same configuration with total 79°, one part 32° and the other x°: x + 32 = 79, so x = 79 − 32 = 47°. Identify the outer arc as the whole in both.

findings.doneWhen: Both directions of the part-whole relationship are explicitly modelled before Question 3.

findings.finding: Vary the given angle to make f and g equal and then reverse their ordering.
findings.breakdown: Students distinguish the sizes of the sectors labelled 4f and 2g from the values of f and g.
findings.checked: With given angle 120°, 4f = 120 and 2g = 60, giving f = g = 30. With 100°, f = 25 and g = 40. These use the same taught relationships and algebra as the existing task.
findings.assumptions: Each replacement changes only the given angle in the existing diagram.

repair.proposal: Append (b) Replace 130° with 120°. Find f and g. [f = 30, g = 30] (c) Replace 130° with 100°. Which is larger, f or g? [f = 25, g = 40, so g is larger.]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing diagram and retains its coefficient labels.

findings.finding: The introductory co-interior example uses an additive one-step equation without an opening review of solving that equation.
findings.breakdown: Recognising the co-interior pair gives 128 + x = 180; isolating x is a substantial prior algebraic step, and the worked example goes directly to 52.
findings.checked: p22 and p28 establish earlier equation solving, but the immediately preceding transversals topic rehearses positional identification rather than solving equations. The supplied parallel-line teaching contains no opening review.
findings.assumptions: One-step equation solving is prior knowledge. No calculator is assumed; the missing recall is the inverse operation.

repair.proposal: Before p52-transversal, add: “Find the unknown angle; all values are in degrees. (a) x + 65 = 180; (b) 112 + y = 180; (c) z + 47 = 180.” Answers: x = 115°, y = 68°, z = 133°. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse the subtraction step before following p52-example-right.

findings.finding: The opening partial demonstrations require collecting terms and solving linear equations without an opening algebra review.
findings.breakdown: Students must simplify t − 30 + 60 and x + x + 10 + 90, then solve the resulting equations. These algebraic decisions can block the angle reasoning.
findings.checked: Earlier p22 and p28 supply equation methods, including collecting repeated unknowns and solving two-step equations. The immediately preceding formal-reasoning teaching and supplied practice rehearse numerical angle relationships and additive unknowns, rather than collecting repeated unknowns and solving two-step equations. No teaching or review blocks are supplied for the angle-equations topic.
findings.assumptions: Collecting terms and solving linear equations are prior algebra knowledge, consistent with the earlier booklet examples and the separate algebra course booklets. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p68-q1, add: (a) Simplify x + x + 10 + 90. [2x + 100] (b) Solve t + 30 = 90. [t = 60] (c) Solve 2a + 10 = 70. [a = 30] (d) Solve 3b + 2b + 20 = 120. [b = 20]. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students briefly rehearse collecting terms and solving the required equation forms before the partial angle demonstrations.

findings.finding: Change both half-angle expressions to preserve x while changing the whole angle.
findings.breakdown: Students distinguish the solution of the equality from the angle size obtained by substitution.
findings.checked: Originally 6x − 14 = 3x + 4 gives x = 6 and two 22° halves. The proposed labels give 6x − 8 = 3x + 10, again x = 6, with two 28° halves and total 56°. All angles are valid, and the method matches the existing question.
findings.assumptions: Students have completed p71-q8 using its stated equal-halves condition.

repair.proposal: Append (a) OB still bisects ∠AOC, but the half-angle labels become (6x − 8)° and (3x + 10)°. Find x. [6] (b) Find the new size of ∠AOC. [56°] (c) Explain why x stays the same while ∠AOC increases by 12°. [Both half-angle expressions increased by 6°, preserving their equality at the same x; the two halves together increase by 12°.]

findings.doneWhen: The three optional parts follow p71-q8 and use its existing bisector configuration.

findings.finding: Generalise the distinction between alternative names and distinct geometrical objects.
findings.breakdown: The existing question contrasts coincident rays with different segments; counting all objects extends that comparison naturally.
findings.checked: For collinear P, Q, R in that order, the six ordered names determine one line, four rays and three segments. The definitions and p4-q3 supply the required methods.
findings.assumptions: P, Q and R are distinct, with Q between P and R.

repair.proposal: After p4-q3-b, optionally ask: 'Using two different letters from P, Q and R, name every distinct line, ray and segment. Group names for the same object and explain.' Expected: one line with six names; four rays, PQ=PR, RP=RQ, QP and QR; three segments, PQ=QP, PR=RP and QR=RQ.

findings.doneWhen: The task distinguishes names from objects and includes the correct grouping.

findings.finding: Question 3 requires relating a whole angle to its adjacent component sectors, but preceding instruction does not supply that relationship.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise which label measures the whole angle and decide whether to add component measures or subtract a known component. The adjacency definition supplies positional conditions, without explaining this numerical relationship.
findings.checked: p5 and p6 identify whole-angle boundaries across internal arms but do not calculate measures. p10-q9-c–e already require sector addition, but provide no instructional cue or demonstration. p16 adds measures of separate angles for classification; p19 teaches adjacency only. General whole-angle addition and subtraction are not modelled before p21-q3.
findings.assumptions: This finding assumes angle decomposition has not been taught separately; retained context question q2 checks that assumption. Basic arithmetic is prior knowledge; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p21-q3, state: 'The measure of a whole angle is the sum of its adjacent parts.' Show sectors 32° and 47° inside a whole angle t°: t=32+47=79°. Then show a whole angle of 79°, one part 47° and the other x°: x+47=79, so x=79−47=32°. Explicitly identify the whole and its parts.

findings.doneWhen: Students see both finding a whole angle and finding a missing component modelled before Question 3, unless separate prior teaching establishes this method.

findings.finding: Distinguish adjacency from complementarity and supplementarity.
findings.breakdown: The task connects consecutive topics while separating a positional relationship from relationships between measures.
findings.checked: All three requested configurations exist: adjacent sectors 30° and 60°, 70° and 110°, and 40° and 60°. Definitions in p16 and p19 suffice.
findings.assumptions: Drawn sectors share a vertex and an arm without overlapping.

repair.proposal: After p20-q2, optionally ask: 'Draw and label (a) adjacent complementary angles, (b) adjacent supplementary angles, and (c) adjacent angles that are neither. Must adjacent angles be complementary or supplementary? Explain.' Expected examples: 30° and 60°; 70° and 110°; 40° and 60°. No: adjacency describes position, whereas complementarity and supplementarity describe totals.

findings.doneWhen: Students provide valid configurations and explain why adjacency alone does not determine the sum.

findings.finding: Justify vertically opposite equality using straight-angle relationships.
findings.breakdown: Students explain an established rule using previously taught relationships rather than measurement.
findings.checked: For two distinct intersecting lines, an angle c adjacent to both opposite angles gives a+c=180 and b+c=180, hence a=b. p22 supplies the straight-angle relationship and p32 supplies opposite-angle identification.
findings.assumptions: The two lines are distinct and intersect.

repair.proposal: After p34-q5, optionally ask: 'Two straight lines intersect. Label one angle a°, its vertically opposite angle b°, and an angle adjacent to both c°. Explain why a=b without measuring.' Expected: a+c=180 and b+c=180, so a=180−c=b.

findings.doneWhen: The explanation derives opposite-angle equality from the two straight-angle equations.

findings.finding: Parts b and i repeat the same whole parallelism task without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both ask for a parallelism decision and justification from the same 124° and 46° co-interior givens in the same configuration.
findings.checked: Compared the shared stem, complete parts, supplied diagram descriptions, angle positions and givens. Both have two descending steep lines crossed by a descending transversal, six continuation arrows, and the same marked interior sectors. No retrieval or comparison instruction explains the repetition.
findings.assumptions: The supplied diagram specifications represent the repeated configuration accurately.
findings.doneWhen: Question 6 contains one copy of the 124° and 46° co-interior parallelism task.

findings.finding: Generalise the angle between the bisectors of adjacent angles.
findings.breakdown: The existing equal-angle pairs provide the structure needed to explain when the two bisecting rays are perpendicular.
findings.checked: For positive adjacent angles a and b with total θ<360°, the smaller angle between their internal bisectors is a/2+b/2=θ/2. It equals 90° exactly when θ=180°. The existing question supplies equal halves, and earlier teaching supplies angle addition.
findings.assumptions: Both angles are positive, have disjoint interiors and together span less than a complete turn.

repair.proposal: After p77-q22, optionally ask: 'Two positive adjacent angles total θ°, where 0<θ<360. Draw a ray dividing each angle into two equal parts. Find the smaller angle between these rays, explain your answer, and state when they are perpendicular.' Expected: θ/2, because the intervening halves sum to a/2+b/2; perpendicular exactly when θ=180°.

findings.doneWhen: The task states its angle conditions and derives both θ/2 and the perpendicularity condition.
